e-9087.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A = PJP^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $\det(A-\lambda I)=0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ 2 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(-2-\lambda )-4\cdot 2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -18 & =0 \\ (\lambda -6)(\lambda +3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 2 \\ -6 & -1\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix. 

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}6-\lambda  & 2 \\ -6 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (6-\lambda )(-1-\lambda )-(2)(-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +6 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, and a Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{1}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(3)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

EXPLANATION

Every n×n matrix A can be written in the form

A=PJP−1,

where J is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of A, and P is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix J, we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix A by solving det(A−λI)=0:

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 2x2 Matrix With Two Distinct Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 2 \\ -6 & -1\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix. 

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}6-\lambda  & 2 \\ -6 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (6-\lambda )(-1-\lambda )-(2)(-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +6 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, and a Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{1}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(3)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}8 & 6 \\ 4 & -2\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 6 \\ 4 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(-2-\lambda )-(6)(4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda -40 & =0 \\ (\lambda -10)(\lambda +4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=10.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, and a Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{1}(-4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(10)=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 10\end{aligned}].
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 2x2 Matrix With Two Distinct Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}8 & 6 \\ 4 & -2\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 6 \\ 4 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(-2-\lambda )-(6)(4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda -40 & =0 \\ (\lambda -10)(\lambda +4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=10.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, and a Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{1}(-4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(10)=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 10\end{aligned}].
$$

decision.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is (1-λ)(-2-λ)-4=λ²+λ-6=(λ+3)(λ-2). The distinct eigenvalues -3 and 2 imply that A is diagonalizable, so diag(-3,2) is a Jordan canonical form.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(-2-\lambda )-(2)(2) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -6 & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, and a Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{1}(-3)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 5 \\ -10 & -9\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix. 

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}6-\lambda  & 5 \\ -10 & -9-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (6-\lambda )(-9-\lambda )-(5)(-10) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, and a Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{1}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-4)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 2x2 Matrix With Two Distinct Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 5 \\ -10 & -9\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix. 

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}6-\lambda  & 5 \\ -10 & -9-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (6-\lambda )(-9-\lambda )-(5)(-10) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, and a Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{1}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-4)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ 1 & 8\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & -2 \\ 1 & 8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(8-\lambda )-(-2)(1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +42 & =0 \\ (\lambda -7)(\lambda -6) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=7$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, and a Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{1}(7)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(6)=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]

EXPLANATION

Every n×n matrix A can be written in the form A=PJP−1, where J is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of A, and P is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix J, we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix A by solving det(A−λI)=0:

|5−λ−218−λ|=0(5−λ)(8−λ)−(−2)(1)=0λ2−13λ+42=0(λ−7)(λ−6)=0

So, the eigenvalues are λ1=7 and λ2=6. Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix A is diagonalizable, and a Jordan canonical form is

J=J1(7)⊕J1(6)=[7006]

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 2x2 Matrix With Two Distinct Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ 1 & 8\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & -2 \\ 1 & 8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(8-\lambda )-(-2)(1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +42 & =0 \\ (\lambda -7)(\lambda -6) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=7$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, and a Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{1}(7)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(6)=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix. 

Notice that $A$ is a scalar matrix, which means that it is already in Jordan canonical form. Therefore, it has a single (repeated) eigenvalue $\lambda =-4,$ and

$$
J=A=-4I=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix. 

Notice that $A$ is a scalar matrix, which means that it is already in Jordan canonical form. Therefore, it has a single (repeated) eigenvalue $\lambda =8,$ and

$$
J=A=8I=[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

A=PJP−1,

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix. 

Notice that $A$ is a scalar matrix, which means that it is already in Jordan canonical form. Therefore, it has a single (repeated) eigenvalue $\lambda =5,$ and

$$
J=A=5I=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix. 

Notice that $A$ is a scalar matrix, which means that it is already in Jordan canonical form. Therefore, it has a single (repeated) eigenvalue $\lambda =-2,$ and

$$
J=A=-2I=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 10
?

Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix A=[1001].

a
[−110−1]
b
[1001]
c
[0100]
d
[−100−1]
e
[1101]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every n×n matrix A can be written in the form

A=PJP−1,

where J is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of A, and P is an invertible matrix.

Notice that A is a scalar matrix, which means that it is already in Jordan canonical form. Therefore, it has a single (repeated) eigenvalue λ=1, and

J=A=I=[1001].

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 2x2 Scalar Matrix
content.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix. 

Notice that $A$ is a scalar matrix, which means that it is already in Jordan canonical form. Therefore, it has a single (repeated) eigenvalue $\lambda =1,$ and

$$
J=A=I=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

decision.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is (10-λ)(8-λ)+1=(λ-9)². Since A≠9I, it is not diagonalizable and has one Jordan block of size 2 with eigenvalue 9. Thus option b is its Jordan canonical form.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}10 & -1 \\ 1 & 8\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix. 

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & -1 \\ 1 & 8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )(8-\lambda )-(-1)\cdot 1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-18\lambda +81 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -9) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=9.$ 

Since $A$ is not a scalar matrix, we conclude that $A$ is not diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{2}(9)=[\begin{aligned}9 & 1 \\ 0 & 9\end{aligned}].

EXPLANATION

Every n×n matrix A can be written in the form

A=PJP−1,

where J is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of A, and P is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix J, we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix A by solving det(A−λI)=0:

|10−λ−118−λ|=0(10−λ)(8−λ)−(−1)⋅1=0λ2−18λ+81=0(λ−9)(λ−9)=0

Therefore, the eigenvalues are λ1=λ2=9.

Since A is not a scalar matrix, we conclude that A is not diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

J=J2(9)=[9109].

verification.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is (λ-9)². Since A-9I is nonzero and has rank 1, the eigenspace has dimension 1, requiring one size-2 Jordan block. Thus option b is correct, agreeing with the revealed solution; the incorrect submission selected option d.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 2x2 Matrix With Only One Eigenvalue
content.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}10 & -1 \\ 1 & 8\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix. 

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & -1 \\ 1 & 8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )(8-\lambda )-(-1)\cdot 1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-18\lambda +81 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -9) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=9.$ 

Since $A$ is not a scalar matrix, we conclude that $A$ is not diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{2}(9)=[\begin{aligned}9 & 1 \\ 0 & 9\end{aligned}].
$$

decision.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is (-12-λ)(2-λ)+49=λ²+10λ+25=(λ+5)². Since A+5I is nonzero with rank 1, the eigenspace has dimension 1. Therefore the Jordan form is a single size-2 block with eigenvalue -5, which is option b.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-12 & -7 \\ 7 & 2\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-12-\lambda  & -7 \\ 7 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-12-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-(-7)\cdot 7 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +25 & =0 \\ (\lambda +5)(\lambda +5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-5.$ 

Since $A$ is not a scalar matrix, we conclude that $A$ is not diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{2}(-5)=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ -1 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-1\cdot (-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=2.$ 

Since $A$ is not a scalar matrix, we conclude that $A$ is not diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{2}(2)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 2x2 Matrix With Only One Eigenvalue
content.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ -1 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-1\cdot (-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=2.$ 

Since $A$ is not a scalar matrix, we conclude that $A$ is not diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{2}(2)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -4 \\ 1 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(-1-\lambda )-1\cdot (-4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +1 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=1.$ 

Since $A$ is not a scalar matrix, we conclude that $A$ is not diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{2}(1)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

EXPLANATION

Every n×n matrix A can be written in the form A=PJP−1, where J is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of A, and P is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix J, we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix A by solving det(A−λI)=0:

|3−λ−41−1−λ|=0(3−λ)(−1−λ)−1⋅(−4)=0λ2−2λ+1=0(λ−1)(λ−1)=0

Therefore, the eigenvalues are λ1=λ2=1.

Since A is not a scalar matrix, we conclude that A is not diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

J=J2(1)=[1101].

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 2x2 Matrix With Only One Eigenvalue
content.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -4 \\ 1 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(-1-\lambda )-1\cdot (-4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +1 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=1.$ 

Since $A$ is not a scalar matrix, we conclude that $A$ is not diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{2}(1)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$
